speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it may be of interest to the House to read a message from Sir Arthur Currie, General Officer Commanding the Canadian Corps in France, in reply to a message which I had sent to him on August 23. My message was:
Ottawa, August 23, 1917. Lt.-Gen. Sir Arthur Currie,
Headquarters Canadian Corps,
France.
On behalf of all ranks -of our military forces in Canada, I desire 'to extend to you and to the officers and men under your command warmest congratulations upon the splendid manner in which Canadian troops have conducted themselves during the fighting around Lens, in defeating the pick of the German army against heavy odds, and steadfastly holding gains made in the face of desperate and repeated counter-attacks. Canada is prouder than ever of her gallant sons who have so bravely and determinedly maintained her honour. We mourn with you the loss of many brave comrades.
Sir Edward Kemp.
I received this morning the following answer from General Sir Arthur Currie:
Sir Edward Kemp,
Minister of Militia,
Ottawa, Canada. *
Your message of congratulation is sincerely appreciated by all ranks Canadian corps. Tell our comrades in the Canadian militia that in addition to winning and consolidating ground of great tactical value, we have inflicted casualties on the foe at least treble our own. -In repeated and determined counter-attacks the flower of the German army was thrown against us, hut our line remained unshaken as our own Rockies. Will not the pride which you say Canada has in her sons inspire her to send us men to take the place of those so nobly fallen.	.
Lt.-Gen. Sir Arthur Currie, General Officer Commanding Canadian Corps in France.

speechtext: The House resumed the adjourned debate on the proposed motion of the- Hon. Mr. Doherty (Minister of Justice) for the third reading of Bill No. 127, the Military Voters' Act, 1917.

maintopic: MILITARY VOTERS' ACT, 1917. THIRD READING OF THE BILL. '
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was not here when this Bill passed through the committee. Acting on suggestions from this side of the House, the hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) made some amendments which I think are an improvement. At the same time there are wide opportunities still for irregularities by those who are inclined to be irregular. My experience has been that while men may be absolutely honest in business transactions, they sometimes look on things as, what they call, smart in political transactions which are not quite honest. I hope that those charged with the administration of this Bill will not take advantage of their opportunities to commit irregularities. I had hoped that the minister would at least have seen his way clear to have allowed the non-residents who are to vote an opportunity to elect one member at large for themselves which would give the n representation in the House. But, apparently he has not seen his way clear to do so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

That Act could be
amended, I have no doubt. It has been done before. We have the example of Saskatchewan and Alberta.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: They have power to amend their constitution; we have not.

maintopic: MILITARY VOTERS' ACT, 1917. THIRD READING OF THE BILL. '
speechtext: That is exactly what I propose, and I do not see why we could not have that amendment made to the Act. But the minister will know whether that can be done or not. That presents one of the greatest opportunities for irregularity, and I had .hoped that the provision would be so amended that there would not be any opportunity for wrong-doing. However, I suppose the Bill was fully discussed in the committee, and now it is open for the third reading and the confirmation.

It was suggested to me to-day that the oath taken by those who enlist in the Canadian forces might be regarded by aliens as equivalent to naturalization. I am not sure as to the nature of the oath taken by those attesting. It may be an oath of service to the King and probably is. I call the minister's attention to it so that he may give it some consideration with a view to providing some amendment, probably in the 
Senate. It might be well, in Form "B," to put a further question and to ask: "When and where were you naturalized if not born a British subject?"-or something like that. I have not given the matter much thought.

House again in committee on Bill No. 53, respecting insurance-Sir Thomas White-resumed from August 4.-Mr. D. Stewart in the Chair.
On section 142 (b)-Accident and sickness insurance:
, Sir THOMAS WHITE: All the clauses of this Bill have been passed with the exception of 142 (b), which relates to conditions under which the business of accident and sickness insurance is to be carried on by companies obtaining a license under this Act. The section was held over until the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) should be present, and I would ask him to state to the committee the point in which he is particularly interested in connection with it.

The clause which I consider objectionable reads:
(h) if the policy provides that written notice of injury must be given to the company within a specified period after the date of the accident causing such injury, such period shall be not less than thirty days.
At first sight that would appear to be in the interest of the person insured as giving him a longer time to give notice to the company; but my contention is that it is absolutely against the interest of the insured-that is the honest insured-and in favour of the man who has fraudulent intentions. 1 object also to the same clause under subsection 3 on page 55 which relates to casualties through illness. While it appears arbitrary, it must be noticed that there is this further clause applying to both of these clauses, that failure to give such notice within the specified time shall not invalidate the claim if it be shown that it was not reasonably possible to give notice within the time required. I contend that the experience of casualty companies must necessarily be the only safe guide for the House in determining on the safest and best legislation about matters of

this kind. I contend that the natural result of legislation providing for a period of thirty days within which notice may be given in cases of accident, and forbidding the insertion of any other period in a policy, will be to open the door to fraud. Casualty companies are peculiarly susceptible to fraudulent practices by dishonest insuring persons, who at times profit by their dishonesty and also compel companies to charge higher rates to honest insurers, as they are compelled to pay these dishonest claims. In other words, every dishonest claim that goes through increases the cost to the honest person insured. The longer the period for notice of any accident the more opportunities are given for fraud. The honest insurer generally gi\es notice immediately; the dishonest insurer hides his illness and, under this clause in the Bill, the man who is injured so as to incapacitate him for ten days, sees on the face of his policy that he is not required to give notice until the end of thirty days. If he is dishonest, he nurses his illness after he is cured and gets thirty days indemnity where he is rightly entitled to one, two, three, or four days. That is an objectionable feature of this Bill.
I contend that my argument is in favour of both the company and the honest insuring person. We all know that in New York some few years ago there was a perfect plethora of dishonest transactions with insurance companies. It became a great abuse, and the trend of modern legislation, both on the other side of the line and here, is to shorten the period of notice rather than to lengthen it, in order to get at the fraudulent insurer. I contend that it is the duty of the Dominion of Canada, it is the duty of any state, to protect the honest insurer and to differentiate between him and the dishonest one. Under this Bill the period for giving notice of injury cannot be less than thirty days; it is imperative, and no company can insert anything else in its policy. In other words, notice may b given after the injury has long passed away, after the man is better, and it is quite apparent upon the face of it that this will give a great lever to the fraudulent man in putting in a claim to which he is not entitled. That must be computed by the insurance companies in dealing with such claims, and will therefore increase the cost to the honest insurer. The honest insurer has to pay the cost which the companies are put,to in meeting dishonest or fraudulent claims.
The same argument applies to the illness clause. One of the largest companies in Canada in the accident and illness casualty business finds that out of 3,726 claims for accident made upon it from January 16 up .to July 21 of this year, 2,583 claims, or 70 per cent of the total claims for disability, were for less than twenty days duration, and out of 5,074 claims for sickness, 3,476, or GO per cent, were for disabilities of less than fifteen days duration. See the absurdity of inserting an arbitrary clause allowing thirty days in all those cases, where the duration was from twenty to fifteen days. The avenue for fraud is clearly opened up for every one of those cases to nurse the sickness or injury, for fifteen days in one case and ten in the other. I do not say that every case would be fraudulent, but I do say that the practice is vicious; it is not in line with modem legislation, and this Bill is wrong in every place where it lengthens the term of notice. If the minister differs-I do not know that he does; in fact I fancy from what I have seen that he rather inclines to my point of view-but I do think the superintendent of insurance does. I do not like to	speak	about an official of	the
Government but there are some men who are obsessed with theories and are oblivious of facts-and the minister might find a gentleman of that kind in his department. I point out that this particular company, whose name I do not put forward, paid, in 1916, to its policy holders in Canada. $103,948.
It paid 3,726 accident claims, involving $46,887, and 5,744 in sickness claims, involving $57,061. Considering for a moment the triviality of many of these claims, one can see the danger of fixing a minimum period of thirty days, and compelling the insurance companies to state in their own policies, if they give any notices at all, that they are compelled to fix that period of not less than thirty days within which notice of accident must be given. The main object in giving notice of an accident, as I understand, is to give the insurance company a chance to investigate a claim, to send a man upon the spot to see the insured person, and to ascertain the particulars of how, when and where the accident occurred, and I think it is proper that any insurance company should have that notice within a reasonable time. As a matter of fact, I think, generally, throughout Canada, the words used in the statutes are " a reasonable time." But in this Bill the Government is providing what I maintain to be

an unreasonable time, in reference to the class of insurance which these particular clauses are intended to deal with. The lengthening of the period is an incentive and an invitation to fraud. It is as much as to say to the man who is slightly injured: " Come along, you are hurt, it, is* true, but do not tell the company for thirty days, although you are able to get around in three days." That part of it strikes me as very serious. Fraud hurts the company and hurts the insured. Fraudulent persons Sometimes have been known, particularly in the large centres of the United States, to insure for the purpose of having an accident. Companies are up against it, and, as the companies are up against it, they put, in their schedule of rates, an allowance on account of fraud, and, naturally, the honest man taking out insurance has to pay the bill for the fraudulent one. In this case I say it hurts both the company and the man who is injured, if he is honest. The Government does not want to protect the fraudulent man who insures. To my mind the Government's duty is to consider the interests of the honest person who insures, and this provision is standing in the way here, and putting a penalty upon the honest person insuring, in favour of the fraudulent or dishonest man. The trend of modern legislation in matters of this kind is entirely opposite to the course pursued here. I have read the evidence taken before the Banking and Commerce Committee, through whose hands this Bill passed, and, whi'e they discussed other important features of the Bill, there is not a scintilla of evidence upon the record which touches these clauses. I am told the reason the Bill ip introduced in its present shape is that certain insurance companies wanted it that way; that it is a model Bill and.a standard form. Yet no discussion took place about it in the Banking and Commerce Committee, and 1 invite the members of that committee to consider the question now. As I understand it, the trend of modern legislation is diametrically opposed to long terms within which notice must be given, and is equally favourable to the shortening of that term, in the interests of the insuring public. I would suggest to the minister that twenty days for accidents, and fifteen days for illness, would be fair, and yet to my mind it is too long.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Is my hon. friend
satisfied with the provision as to the notice regarding sickness? The notice in -the Bill is fifteen days for sickness.

I .think ten days would oe sufficient. I think notice of twenty days for accidents and ten days for sickness would be about right.' I would be satisfied with the sickness provision, because I can see that sickness will sometimes prevent a man from considering his ordinary business affairs in the same way as a man would who is free from illness. Accidents are notoriously public as a rule, and generally some one is looking after the man who. has met with the accident. An accident brings with it the idea, have you any insurance, more than sickness does, and for that reason I would make a distinction between the two classes of cases, and would suggest twenty days' notice for accidents and ten days' notice for sickness. These are the periods which are fixed in the states of New York, Illinois, Wisconsin, Minnesota, South Dakota, Iowa, Texas, Montana, Oregon and Washington. The hon. Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) will agree with me when I say that in metropolitan centres, such as New York and Chicago, and those large cities, they have had an experience which no city in this country ever had, and their dates have been fixed upon the basis of the experience of the companies in those cities. I have not the general rule in the States, beyond those states I have mentioned, but those states cover the main insuring states, and most populous cities. North Dakota is an exception, that state having a thirty-day provision in case of accident. I do not apprehend that the Minister of Finance would really rather follow North Dakota than New York or Illinois. It would be like following an amateur, instead of a professional, in the business. . But even if he follows North Dakota he would not be Iqng right, because three companies have withdrawn from North Dakota since that law was put in force, and three other companies operating there have threatened to withdraw, and the Commissioner of Insurance, W. C. Taylor, North Dakota, has recently acknowledged that the Bill is a mistake, and is asking for legislation reducing the time.

I have looked over the Bill, and I do not observe that there is any definition as to what shall be deemed to be notice. Would the hon. gentleman be willing, suppose the time were shortened, to treat the mailing of a letter as notice? Because there might be cases where the person resided a long distance from the office of the company, and it would be

difficult to give them notice in the short time allowed. If the mailing of a letter were deemed to be notice, it would make it much easier.

I am under a different
impression, but I think there is something in the Bill in regard to giving notice. As a matter of law I should think that the mailing of a letter is the giving of notice, no matter when it reaches the company, if the mailing of the letter can be proved. The law is that when a letter is. put in the post office it becomes the property of the man to whom it is addressed, and I think that proof, by secondary evidence, that a letter was mailed, would cover the case, notwithstanding the want of a clause of that kind in the Bill. But, with all due deference, I should like to consider that question before I give an out-and-out opinion.
The provision is in the next section.

The hon. gentleman
from Frontenac (Mr. Edvards) tells me that in the following section there is a term regarding the notice; but apart from the United States legislation, let us come nearer home. In the province of Ontario we have w,hat is known as the Workmen's Compensation Act, the product of the mind of one of the most able and skilful members of the judiciary in the province. That Act was' drafted after some two or three years' labour and study by Sir William Meredith, wno so adorns the bench of that province.
Sir William Meredith .made a special study of that Act. He examined all the compensation Acts adopted by other countries, and he worked out a form of legislation admitted by even the United States authorities to be the best, the most complete, and most comprehensive Compensation Act that can be found to-day upon the statute book of any country. Section 20 of that Act goes a good deal further than the provision that I ask for here. That section provides that compensation shall not be payable unless notice of the accident is given as soon as practicable after the happening of it, and before the workman has voluntarily left the employment in which he was injured. It will be observed that - notice is to be given, not quickly, or within thirty days, but as soon as practicable after the accident. Of course, there is a saving clause in subsection 5 of section 20 to protect the honest insured for failure to give the prescribed notice, if the board is of
opinion that the claim for compensation is a just one and ought to be allowed. That language, to my mind, is preferable to the language used in this Bill under section 142B, clause (1). The Workmen's Compensation Act is more drastic in shutting out entirely the claim which the board may deem to be dishonest, and putting an end to it at once on account of failure to give notice as provided in section 20.
To show further the trend of modern legislation, I point to section 99 of the Workmen's Compensation Act, which reads as follows:
Every employer shall within three days after the happening of accident to a workman in his employment notify the Board by registered post of the (a) happening of the accident and nature of it; (b) time of its occurrence; (c) name and address of the workman; (d) place where the accident happened; (e) name and address of the physician or surgeon, if any, by whom the workman was or is attended for the injury. -
Why such care? Why such specific provision in point of time? Moreover, what happens if the employer does not give notice?
Does the hon. gentleman no't realize that there is a great difference between the Workmen's Compensation Act and insurance against injury and accident?

If' there is any difference, it is that in the one case the Government protects against fraud, and that in the other it does not. Why should not this Parliament protect the people who are paying premiums to these companies, just as they protect those who pay under the Workmen's Compensation Act? I cannot see why the Government should protect the people in one case and not in the other. This proposed legislation ought to come closer to the legislation respecting workmen's compensation,' not go further away from it.
For every contravention of section 99, the employer shall incur a penalty of $50. The Act, therefore, is of a drastic nature; it compels the giving of notice quickly, so that the provincial Government may be enabled to look into the case. If that were the case here, the company affected could look into the matter in the same way, I think that the two Acts are on all fours; there is no distinguishing difference that I can see.

Would the Ontario
Workmen's Compensation Act make any provision for the employer's giving the

notice if the injured man was unable to. do so?
It is definitely specified here: every employer shall within three days give such notice.

The employer gives notice if the man is so badly injured that he can not give it himself. But in some cases nobody may know that the injured person is insured; he may be so badly injured that he cannot give notice of the accident within the ten or fifteen days.

This Bill provides that if reasonable cause can be shown why notice was not given, failure to give notice shall not operate against the claim. The section that I have just read comes very close to the point; it should make the minister hesitate to disregard the trend of modern legislation.
There is an abstract argument which enters into this question. The whole body of the insuring public is affected by the morality of that body. The higher the moral standard, the cheaper the insurance; fraud is entirely eliminated if the morale is absolutely good. The shorter the term for notice, the-less opportunity for fraud. The fewer fraudulent claims paid, the cheaper the insurance to the individual. Such provision should be made as would tend to elevate the moral standard and not give opportunity to persons of doubtful intentions to create a bad rather than a good moral atmosphere. I have referred to the fact that this Bill protects the honest insurer; it does seem to me that there should be some drastic method of shutting out the dishonest one.
The provinces have the right to legislate upon such questions as this. I should think that the minister would deem it desirable so to standardize this clause with which I have been dealing that it would cover the whole country. Quebec province has in its code a provision that reasonable notice shall be given in such cases. The provincial courts have "decided that such reasonable notice means twenty days in the case of accident and fifteen days-perhaps not more than ten-in case of illness. In the United States the tendency is not to lengthen the notice; the trend of legislation is rather to shorten it.
1 know a company in Canada that gives for $12, one dollar a month, $40 a month indemnity in case of accident. The other companies in Canada are charging $21 for the same thing. That company informs me 
that if this Bill goes through, they will have to increase their'rates. I do not think the Superintendent of Insurance will deny that; if the minister asks him about it, he will admit it. Under these circumstances, how can the minister justify the increase of the rates against the ihonest insuring public that would result from the provision of the present Bill? I hope that the minister will consider carefully the suggestions that I have made; that he will be guided only by his own good judgment; that he will consider the advisability of amending the Bill -I am prepared to move an amendment if that is necessary-by so changing the clauses in question that the provisions for thirty and fifteen days' notice shall be changed to twenty and fifteen.
The hon. member, I think, misreads the clause. I do not think it is necessary for a man to wait for thirty days before giving notice. He can give notice in thirty minutes, if he so desires.
Certainly.

But this clause prevents a company from shutting out his claim if notice is given within thirty days. Only the companies' are affected by this clause, and if there had been any serious objection on their part to it, we would have heard about the matter while the Bill was before the Banking and Commerce Committee. The mere fact, therefore, that none of the companies made any objection to the clause at that time leads me to think that they do not object to it. I have had nearly twenty years of experience in connection with accident insurance, and I have represented and still represent some of the strongest companies doing business in Canada, but I have never had experience of a company shutting out a claim on account of notice not being given within the required time.
I have sometimes seen notice given two or three months after an accident has occurred. It is just possible that a company might take advantage of that provision to shut out a claim, and I do not think they should be allowed to do so because a person does not give notice within thirty days, but this provision prevents them from shutting out a claim if notice is given within thirty days. That is simply for the protection of the insured. My hon. friend (Mr. Morphy) speaks of fraudulent insurers. No hon. member wants to endorse fraudulence in regard to insurance or any other matter. Many people who may have incurred apparently slight accidents, have later on

been laid up owing to their injuries developing into something serious. Many of them may not give, notice to the company, letting those slight accidents go by default. If they had to give notice within a short time, they might not do so, and the company might take advantage of notice not being given within the prescribed time. During my experience I have never known of any one trying to defraud a company to any extent. Sometimes, when a person has an accident, he may make claim for a few days more than those during which he has been laid up, but nearly all the companies issue policies that cover total disability and partial disability, so that there has, in my experience, never been any trouble in settling claims. Fraud may occur in the larger cities. I distinctly remember the case my hon. friend speaks about which happened in New York. The companies found that a sort of syndicate of fraud had been created there and they took measures to counteract it. In Canada I have never heard of anything of the kind, and we, of course, are legislating .for Canada. I am sorry to hear my hon. friend rather censure the Superintendent of Insurance, because l believe, if there is a capable Civil Servant in Canada to-day, it is the Superintendent of Insurance. Not only does he know his business thoroughly, but he is absolutely upright and straightforward in regard to it. I could not, so far as my experience is concerned, speak too highly of him. The clause, as it stands, is all right, and it ought to pass in its present form.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The particular paragraph of which the hon. member complains is (h) of subclause 2 of section 142 B of the original Bill. I believe it is section 134 of the Bill as reprinted. The particular provision is this:
If the policy provides that written notice of injury must be given to the company within a specified period after the date of the accident causing such injury, such period shall he not less than thirty days.
The intention of this was to protect the insured. I appreciate fully the point made by the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy), namely: That if the effect of this provision would be to cause frauds to such an extent that the rate of accident insurance would rise, it would, of course, not be in the interest of the public. Personally, I have not been of the view that that would he the result of the enactment of this proviso. It is to be borne in mind, in connection with this question of notice under a Dominion Insurance Act, that Canada is a
very large country geographically. I can understand that, in the case of an accident insurance company doing business, say in the state of New York or in the state of Illinois or in any other state of the United States, it might be wise to provide for a shorter period of notice. But giving the matter my best consideration, I thought there was a distinction between the case of a company carrying on business in a state or a province and the case of a company carrying on business in so large a country as the Dominion of Canada. It takes a considerable time to give notice from one part of Canada to another portion which may be separated from it by two or three thousand miles, apd a^tho^gh provision is made in this Dill' for giving notice to an authorized agent of the company, all the public might not be aware of that, and most of them would naturally send their notice to the head office of the company. That is a feature that should be considered. I have an open mind upon the matter, and I would rather invite the opinions of hon. members. We do not want to make a mistake either way. I do not want a provision under which the public will be prejudiced through failing to send in their notices within too brief a time.
On the other hand we certainly do not desire legislation which will encourage fraud. With the permission of the committee, I shall read part of a memorandum I have received from the Superintendent of Insurance dealing with this matter :
One of the clauses contained in the policy is to the effect that the insured shall have 30 days from the date of the accident within which to give notice thereof to the company. This provision conforms with what is the practice at the present time of a considerable number of companies licensed by the department. It may be pointed out that during the last few years there has been a tendency on the part of a number of the companies to increase the time within which notice may be given. Many of the older policies required "immediate notice". Those of a later date required 10 days, 14 days, 20 days, 21 days, and in recent years a number of companies have adapted 30 days. This tendency has been quite marked in practically all companies, and it fs believed that the change is in the interests of the insured. The following companies have filed with the department policy forms containing provision for 30 days notice: Canada Accident Assurance Co., Dominion of Canada Guarantee and Accident Co., Employers' Liability Assurance Corp., Globe Indemnity Co., Maryland Casualty Co., North American Accident Co., Yorkshire Insurance Co. It is true, as stated by the hon. member for North Perth, that the courts in the province of Quebec have ruled that reasonable notice is twenty days. That ruling was given, I suppose, with reference to the Quebec law governing provincially incorporated companies, but it must be borne in mind that our Act is an Act for the Dominion of Canada.
Does the Quebec decision hold that 20 days is the proper construction of the statute, or that the elapse of 20 days would not be unreasonable?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not quite positive, but I think it is a fact that the legislation of the province of Quebec requires reasonable notice to be given, and the courts have held that 20 days is a reasonable notice under that provision.
Did they hold that 20 days would not be unreasonable?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I don't think so.
That's the point.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is to be borne in mind that while most of the companies carry on their business fairly and honourably, our legislation should nevertheless be such that it is not within the power of any company or companies t-o take undue advantage. Cases have been drawn to the' attention of the department in which companies have sought to take advantage of the insured, not because there was any doubt as to the validity of the claim, but because notice had not been given within the time limit specified in the
4 p.m. policy. I should like hon. gentlemen who have had some experience in this matter to give me the benefit of their vietvs, because, as I stated before, I have an open mind on the subject. Our first duty, I think should be to protect the insurers, that is, the public.
Is not that what we are doing in this clause?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is what I said, but the hon. member for North Perth makes this point, and it is worthy of consideration-he says that if the notice is so

long as practically to invite fraudulent claims the companies, being subject to such-fraudulent claims, will necessarily have to raise their rates, and in that way the public will suffer. It is pretty difficult to decide whether the difference of ten days, as be- . tween twenty and thirty, would make so much difference to the companies in the way of having to settle fraudulent claims " that the rates would have to be raised.
Would not " reasonable time " be the best expression of all?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That would leave it open. I think my right hon. friend will agree with me that if we can fix a time that is deemed to be reasonable it would be better to fix it, because otherwise the question of what was a reasonable time would depend upon the point of view of the court, and a man who had suffered an accident, and was insured against accidents, would not know in advance what the court would hold as a reasonable notice, and consequently he might be prejudiced. I do not think we should insert a provision that it should be a " reasonable notice." If this committee can come to a conclusion as to what is a reasonable notice with respect to the filing of claims arising out of accidents in a country such as Canada, I think we should insert that term in the Bill, so as to have it fixed and definite.
My hon. friend has touched upon one other point. He says that many of these companies are provincially incorporated, which is true, and that they might therefore be left to provincial legislation. It is to be pointed out, however, that we are about to license such of these companies as will submit themselves to the provisions of this Act, and take out a license from the superintendent of insurance, and it is open to us to provide, as a condition of their obtaining that license, and for the sake of uniformity in accident and sickness insurance in Canada, that they shall be subject to the provisions of this Act, including among others a limitation as to period of notice.'

I quite agree with the Finance Minister as to what should be the intention of the Act. Personally, I think that thirty days is not an unreasonable limit. I appreciate that we can hardly decide what the law ought to be in respect of sickness and accident policies from our experience with life insurance policies. For a great many years I tried to get fire in-

surance legislation introduced into this Parliament, or at least, I tried to get the officers of the department to admit that we had jurisdiction enough to get the kind of law I wanted with regard to fire insurance policies; but I did not succeed. My experience with insurance companies has been that there was not sufficient time, or their regulations were so framed as to prejudice the insured on account of technicalities. My professional experience, of course, has been more largely concerned with fire insurance cases than life and accident cases. I remember that I lost the first case I ever had against a fire insurance company, because it was provided that proof of loss must be filed within fourteen days. In this case proof of loss was not filed until the seventeenth day, but the court held that I was right and I got a verdict, but I lost the case on appeal. I have had many other cases; some I have lost on that very ground, and in others I have had a very close call. Quite a number of years ago the legislature of Ontario adopted the standard clause, and practically all the other provinces have followed in providing that proof of loss shall be filed as early as can reasonably be done, or some words to that effect. The courts of the different provinces have held that in some cases thirty days was a reasonable time and they have even gone so far as to hold that sixty days was not unreasonable. I had a case within the last ten years in which our own courts held that fifty-nine days was reasonable under the circumstances. I would not want to see this time limited. I do not know that I would advocate extending it beyond thirty days because there is a difference of principle between fire insurance companies and accident companies. I'f a building is destroyed by fire it is destroyed so that if damage is done it is there and it can be seen at one time as well as another; whereas, in the case of an accident company, it is quite possible that a man may receive an accident and within thirty days the man would have recovered and the insurance company would have no opportunity of examination. I presume that is the point that the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) has raised. I think it would be a mistake to limit this time co a period under thirty days. Any man ought to have at least thirty days in which to give notice. There are not many cases of fraud and there are few cases in which companies wish to contest claims. They are surrounded by suf-320
ficient protection. The claimant must prove his case on some reasonable evidence. He cannot go into court, and say: I was sick, or I was injured, or laid .up, for two or three weeks. He has to produce some kind of proof. He may have to produce medical proof. I do not say that he necessarily must do all that, but in the ordinary course of business in proving a case in court, we have to give evidence of some kind. Therefore, I do not think a delay of thirty days would prejudice the ease or that the company would not be in a position to protect itself. I take it to be the principal object of giving notice that it puts the company in a position to make an investigation tif it chooses to do so. If I were going to err at all, I would want to err in favour of the insured. Cases of fraud are very few and what is proposed by the hon. gentleman, I am afraid, would militate against the insured in order to protect a company against a possible case of fraud. I think the clause as it now stands is reasonable.

I think the minister is correct in stating that a time limit of at least thirty days is in favour of the insurer. On the other hand, if what the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) says is correct, his suggestions are both in favour of the insured as well as the insurance companies. If the insurance companies have to raise their rates on account of fraud being practised under this particular section, the persons getting insurance would have to pay an increased premium. But we have the statement of the Minister of Finance that the insurance companies themselves are the best judges of whether an increased time limit for giving notice will tend to fraud and thus force them to increase their permiums. The fact that there are seven companies, licensed under the Dominion Insurance Act, who have, of their own volition, limited the time within which notice was to be given to thirty days, and one to three months, is some evidence that these insurance companies do not share the opinion of the hon. member for North Perth. As regards the ground taken by the hon. member for Carle ton, N.B., (Mr. Carvell) that perhaps there should be no time limit-
I did not say that.

That reasonable notice
should be given-

I did not say that; I
said that thirty days was treasonable.

With regard to the provincial statutes, which have these words " within a reasonable time " in them, if my hon. friend from North Perth looks at the 'Supreme Court reports for the province of Quebec, he will find, in the case he mentioned in which the judges decided that twenty days was a reasonable notice, and the decision was based on the circumstances surrounding that particular case. He will find a case from that province in which it was held that 78 days was a reasonable time because the insured, was not in a position before the 78th day to give notice to the company. So that I do not think that this Quebec case is going to carry you very far. Each particular case is based on the circumstances by which it is surrounded. I do not think that thirty days is a sufficient time. There have been many cases in which the public have been defrauded and not the company. I think that even if this legislation only provided for twenty days the public would still be protected because the next paragraph says that,
Failure to give such notice within the time provided in the policy shall not invalidate the claim if it shall be shown that it was not reasonably possible to give such notice within such time, and that notice was given as soon as was reasonably possible.
Therefore, I do not think it makes much difference whether it is twenty or thirty days.
Does the minister not think I am right in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is right in stating that the policy would not be invalidated even if the notice was given beyond the thirty days provided it would be shown that it was not reasonably possible to give such notice within such time. But it would be a question of fact as to whether it was reasonably possible or not. It is difficult to say just how the court would construe that.
That would be a case of dispute.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

I cannot see that the provision as to thirty days is going to breed fraud in connection with this matter. If I thought so I would be one of the last persons who would uphold the section, but I cannot see it in view of the action of these accident companies themselves in allowing the extended time. As the section stands it suits me all right.

My hon. friend from North Perth (Mr. Morphy) has directed attention to the fact that there was not much discus, sion on these subsections when the Bill was before the Banking and Commerce Committee. My recollection is that upon the day that these subsections were under discussion I was the acting chairman. I think the reason there was so little discussion was that the representatives of the accident insurance companies who were present and taking an active part in the discussion in reference to the other sections were agreed that thirty days was a fair compromise as between the insured and the insurer as to the time within which notice should be given of accident, and that fifteen days was a fair time within which notice should be given of sickness. I think the committee approached the subject in the light that insurance was for the benefit of the insured and not primarily for the benefit pf the company, and that regulations should not be of such drastic character that by too rigid advantage being taken of the time limit the companies might escape liability. They also regarded the subject from the point of view that the giving of the notice after recovery from them did not deprive a company of the opportunity of making inquiry and of satisfying itself as to the extent of the injury. If I understand it, the company always has a right to demand that proof be given of an injury suffered, or of the duration of an illness, or the time when a man was laid up as the result of an accident. It may demand proof from the members of the family; it may demand proof of those who saw the accident, and it may require that the evidence of the medical practitioner who was in attendance be given as to the extent of the injury.
Looking at it from the practical standpoint, cases have come under my notice of men receiving what they thought were trifling injuries which subsequently developed into something very much more serious. But on presenting their claims to the company, they were put out of court and the claims not recognized as notice had not been given within the time provided.
I think the object of this committee should be to hold a balance fairly between the company and the insured, and reviewing all the facts as they have been advanced by various members this afternoon, I do not think much injury will be done to the insurance companies by leaving the terms thirty days and fifteen days, and I certainly think there are cases in which it

will be honestly to the advantage of the insured.

The hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) says that his mind is made up by the figures given by the Finance Minister. Those figures were that twelve companies had expressed a preference for a period of notice running from fourteen to twenty-one days; three had filed a preference for fourteen to fifteen days; five of twenty days and two of twenty-one days. There were only seven companies in favour of a requirement of 30 days' notice as against twelve who favoured a notice of twenty-one, twenty, fifteen or fourteen days.
The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carroll) spoke of the necessity of giving proof. There is no danger that the man who goes out to be fraudulent will not have his proofs ready. That was well shown in the New York frauds. They even went out to have the accident made; they had the motor car burned, they had the witnesses all on hand -some of them strangers whom they had never seen before. Everything was in complete order. The proof will always be ready when the fraudulent man undertakes to deceive; he is in it for the business. It is all right to say that we have not much fraud of this kind in this country; but if the hon. members ask the companies they will find that there is any amount of it, especially in the larger centres, and the companies do complain, and I think with great cause.
Would the evil complained of, as in the automobile case, be remedied by having a shorter period of notice?

The fraud would not be perpetrated so easily. With the longer term, opportunity is given to prepare the evidence and get everything shipshape.
As to the suggestion of the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) about holding the balance evenly, there is only one way to hold it and that is to do a good turn to the company by lessening existing fraud, which will enable the company to give insurance to the public at a cheaper price and at the same time protect the honest insurer from the payments out by the company to fraudulent claimants. It is easily seen that every fraudulent claim paid out increases the cost of insurance to the honest insurer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This matter appears to have been considered by the Banking and Commerce Committee, and as the
329J
consensus of opinion here appears to be in favour of the proviso as it stands, I do not feel that I would be justified in suggesting any change.

Amendments agreed to, section as amended agreed to.
On the schedule.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I may say to the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugs-ley) that the superintendent of insurance has gone most carefully into the checking of all references and cross references. We believe that the Bill now is accurate in respect of the numbering and references and other matters so essential in a Bill of this kind. The Bill and schedule have been reprinted, and the sections renumbered.

Has the minister any
information as to whether or not the New York Life Insurance Company has a federal charter?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yee.

The reason I ask is that I find they have been holding up a lot of insurance on soldiers killed at the front, and I want to take the matter up. I do not know whether it has been brought to the attention of the department or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If -the hon. member has a special interest in this matter, he had better speak to the Superintendent of Insurance. I think there is a regulation which covers the case.

Trade and Commerce-Salaries, rents, wages and contingencies, under Canada Grain Act. Further amount required, $75,000.

I then tcok the matter up with the mayor ot Sydney and one or two other prominent men, and they all wrote to say that they did not desire any donation, that the company was^ making ample provision for the dependents of the men who had lost- 'iieir lives.
